verdict: Caution: lend selectively to downstream service and fabrication SMEs tied to MRPL's operations, not to refining-margin plays; the local blast and national output contraction outweigh Karnataka's GST and power tailwinds.
title: Mangaluru Petroleum Refining & Coal Products: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What this business physically is
**Mangaluru's refining cluster is essentially one anchor plant — MRPL — plus a ring of SMEs that sell it labour, fabrication, transport, catalyst handling and maintenance.** The anchor turns crude into fuels and petrochemicals; the SMEs turn their own inputs (steel, manpower, spares, diesel) into service cash, invoiced monthly against work orders. Value sits in the anchor's margin; cash sits in the SME's receivable from the anchor. **So when a proposal lands, check who the end debtor is; if it is MRPL or a main contractor, ask for the work-order and past payment record.**

## Where cash and risk sit now
**The anchor's numbers look strong on paper — Q3 FY26 revenue ₹29,720 crore, PBT ₹2,214 crore, PAT ₹1,445 crore, debt-equity improved to 0.63 [1] — but a late-September explosion at the Mangaluru refinery injured eight workers [1] and has since claimed a second life, with ₹1.2 crore compensation reported [2][3].** That is a local safety and shutdown risk, not a margin story. Nationally, IIP for NIC 19 output is -0.6% YoY and -0.9% Apr-to-date [D], so the sector's physical volumes are flat-to-down even as peer refiners report margin-led profit (HPCL GRM US$32.2/bbl [7]; BPCL and IOC beats [4][6]). **Separate these: peer profits are margin and inventory gains, not volume growth — do not read them as demand for your borrower's services.**

## The growth opportunity
**Karnataka itself is running ahead of India — GST collections +11.1% Apr-to-date vs +6.1%, and electricity demand +23.3% vs +9.5% [D] — so pursue borrowers serving the plant's utilities, power, fabrication and maintenance spend rather than fuel marketing.** Target SME fabricators, mechanical and electrical maintenance contractors, catalyst and chemical handlers, and logistics tied to the refinery's offtake. **Avoid pure trading of petroleum products and any borrower whose sole collateral is refined stock — price and inventory swings are the anchor's risk, not a lender's.**

## How to grow safely
**Structure against the work order, not the balance sheet: invoice-discounted receivables from MRPL or tier-one contractors, with a margin and a cap per debtor.** Take monthly: work-order status, billing and collection statement, GST returns, and a site-safety compliance certificate. **If the borrower's receivable days stretch beyond the contract terms, ask for the anchor's payment advice before enhancing.** Rating reports note refiners' cash generation supports debt service over 12-18 months [8], but that comfort does not pass automatically to suppliers.

## Early-warning signs
**Watch for work-order cancellations or deferrals after the blast, delayed MRPL payments, and any borrower whose revenue depends on a single contract.** Also track monthly GST turnover against bank credits; a widening gap means diversion. **If a borrower reports a plant shutdown or safety notice, freeze enhancement and re-assess.**
watch: Monthly GST returns vs bank credits
Turnover gap >10% for two months -> ask for debtor ledger and hold enhancement
Receivable days stretch beyond contract -> seek anchor payment advice before renewal
Cancellation or deferral post-blast -> reduce limit or exit
Any shutdown notice -> freeze fresh disbursal and re-assess
Continued negative YoY -> tighten new-to-bank SME limits
